Translating ribosomes protect RNA against termination by sterically preventing Rho's access to the transcript (Probable). During translocation Rho remains bound to the Rut sites via the PBS, while translocating 3' along the RNA, providing evidence for a 'tethered tracking' mechanism (PubMed:25662222, PubMed:25999346, PubMed:7509071). RNA-dependent NTPase which hydrolyzes all four ribonucleoside triphosphates (PubMed:138681). In vitro in the absence of RNA polymerase has (d)ATP-dependent-hydrolysis and 5'-3' helicase activity on RNA:DNA hybrids, releasing RNA from the duplex; has no activity on DNA:DNA substrates (PubMed:1716628, PubMed:25662222, PubMed:25999346, PubMed:3030561, PubMed:34023400, PubMed:40808302). The relevance of Rho's RNA:DNA helicase activity to its in vivo function(s) or mechanism of action remains uncertain (Probable). A catalytically inactive open hexameric ring binds C-rich Rut sites on RNA via its primary-binding site (PBS) located in the protein's N-terminal surface; each protomer can bind a single pyrimidine-C dinucleotide (PubMed:10230401, PubMed:12859904, PubMed:17081977, PubMed:36697824). Concerted rotational changes between each of the six subunits convert from an open conformation favorable to RNA loading to the closed conformation around RNA capable of translocation (PubMed:17081977)

Plays a major role in reduction of R-loop formation across the genome; R-loops can be generated by annealing of untranslated (often antisense) RNA to upstream DNA (PubMed:23251031, PubMed:29474582). Reduction of R-loop formation may explain why Rho is essential (Probable)

The homohexamer assembles into a catalytically inactive open ring structure; the active homohexamer is a closed ring which encircles RNA (PubMed:10230401, PubMed:12859904, PubMed:15642265, PubMed:19879839, PubMed:2461932, PubMed:36697824, PubMed:9586995). texts.value: Catalyzes the reduction of quinones (PubMed:14766567). Acts by simultaneous two-electron transfer, avoiding formation of highly reactive semiquinone intermediates and producing quinols that promote tolerance of H(2)O(2). Quinone reduction is probably the primary biological role of ChrR (By similarity). Can also reduce toxic chromate to insoluble and less toxic Cr(3+). Catalyzes the transfer of three electrons to Cr(6+) producing Cr(3+) and one electron to molecular oxygen without producing the toxic Cr(5+) species and only producing a minimal amount of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Chromate reduction protects the cell against chromate toxicity, but is likely a secondary activity (PubMed:14766567, PubMed:17088379, PubMed:22558308). Can also reduce potassium ferricyanide, 2,6-dichloroindophenol, V(5+), Mo(6+), methylene blue, cytochrome c and U(6+) (PubMed:14766567, PubMed:17088379). During chromate reduction, is able to use both NAD or NADP equally well (PubMed:14766567)
